why.title: 発酵由来のカロテノイドを一段落で解説
why.answer: 発酵由来のカロテノイドとは、特定の酵母または微藻の菌株を密閉型バイオリアクターで培養し、その色素を抽出・精製して得られる着色分子です。この製造ルートは収穫と季節収量を方程式から取り除きます。同じ菌株と同じ発酵プロトコルを使えば、ロットごとに同じ含量値と同じ色相が得られ、生産は一年中途切れずに続きます。製剤にとってこれは、パイロットタンクでも 10 トン規模でも挙動を予測できる色調を意味します。

faq.title: 製剤からよく寄せられる質問

items.q: 発酵由来のアスタキサンチンと Haematococcus 由来のアスタキサンチンの違いは何ですか？
items.a: どちらも同一の活性成分である 3S,3′-S アスタキサンチンを提供します。違いは製造ルートとコストです。Phaffia rhodozyma 由来の酵母アスタキサンチンは密閉発酵槽で製造されるため年中供給でき、有効成分 1 kg 当たりのコストが低く、目標含量に合わせて調整できます。Haematococcus pluvialis は屋外で培養して収穫するため、有効成分 1 kg 当たりのコストは高いものの、単一の十分に特性化された原料を前提とする場合に、多くのバイヤーが基準品として挙げるのがこちらです。仕様が目標色と価格であれば酵母が有利です。特定の由来に紐づく公開臨床データが必要であれば、藻類がより安全な参照になります。

items.q: 全ロットに COA と MSDS をもらえますか。
items.a: はい。すべてのロットに、同一性、含量、重金属、微生物、残留溶媒をカバーする分析証明書と MSDS を同梱して出荷します。欧州（Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008）、米国、日本、韓国の申請に必要な法規書類は、ご要望に応じて提供します。

items.q: 最小発注数量はどのくらいですか。
items.a: 標準グレードは 1 kg です。色合わせ、安定性、官能評価を含む完全なベンチ試験に十分な量です。より大きな数量は用途と数量に応じてお見積りします。適格な申請者には最大 5 シリーズ分のサンプルを無償で、7 日以内に発送します。

items.q: これらの色素はどれくらい安定ですか。
items.a: 遊離型カロテノイドは光、酸素、熱に敏感です。当社は酸化防止剤システム、不透明包装、さらに用途が許す場合の油分散型やマイクロカプセル化のグレードにより、配合段階で対応します。全ロットに 40 °C、相対湿度 75 % での加速安定性データを添付し、アプリケーションチームが配合物に適合したグレードをご提案します。

items.q: 数量を確定する前にサンプルをいただけますか。
items.a: はい。評価に必要なシリーズ、グレード、数量をお知らせください。適格な案件には、各シリーズ 100 g ずつ、最大 5 シリーズ分を無償で、追跡付きの国際輸送にて発送します。評価後も、配合調整のために技術担当者を担当として継続します。

items.q: カスタム発酵製品を開発できますか。
items.a: はい。カスタム菌株開発、含量目標、キャリア、エンカプセル化はすべて対応可能です。研究開発チームは菌株選抜と発酵の最適化を社内で実施し、プロセス開発では大学と連携しています。目標色、用途、数量、納期をお知らせいただければ、実現可能性の見解と開発計画をご返答します。

stories.metaDescription: Where natural pigments come from — biology, history, the people behind them.
stories.title: Color Stories
stories.subtitle: Every pigment has a plant (or a microbe), a place, and a person behind it.

indigo.title: Indigo — Blue from a Leaf
indigo.lede: For three thousand years, blue came from one plant.
indigo.body: Indigofera leaves don't contain blue. They contain indican — a colourless precursor that oxidises into the deep indigo we recognise only after the leaf is crushed, fermented, and exposed to air.

saffron.title: Saffron — A Field of Red
saffron.lede: One hectare of saffron yields about ten kilograms of dried spice.
saffron.body: Each saffron crocus blooms for a single morning. The red threads are hand-picked from each flower — roughly 150 flowers per gram of dried saffron — which is why it's the most expensive spice on Earth.

beetroot.title: Beetroot — Pink That Won't Quit
beetroot.lede: Betanin is one of the rare natural pigments that survives heat.
beetroot.body: Most plant pigments break down when heated. Betanin — the pigment that makes beetroot red — actually becomes more vivid under heat, which is why it's the workhorse of pink and magenta in plant-based food.

spirulina.title: Spirulina — Blue from a Cyanobacterium
spirulina.lede: Phycocyanin gives spirulina its blue colour.
spirulina.body: Cyanobacteria were among the first oxygen-producing life forms on Earth. Phycocyanin, the blue pigment they share with spirulina, is one of the few natural blues that survives both heat and a neutral pH.

turmeric.title: Turmeric — The Gold That Needs Oil
turmeric.lede: Curcumin is almost insoluble in water and fat-soluble in almost everything else.
turmeric.body: The pigment that makes turmeric golden is curcumin, and it behaves like an oil-soluble molecule in every way that matters. Its hue — a warm, slightly orange gold — comes from a conjugated chain that dissolves into the fat phase rather than the water phase, which is why a pinch of turmeric powder in water turns yellow-brown while a pinch in milk turns properly gold. That single solubility fact decides most of what a formulator needs to know about it, and it is also why the same pigment has to be carried in an oil-dispersible form rather than a water-dispersible one.

chlorophyll.title: Chlorophyll — The Colour of a Leaf
chlorophyll.lede: The only green most of us will ever use comes from a molecule held together by a single metal ion.
chlorophyll.body: Chlorophyll is a porphyrin ring with a magnesium ion in the middle, and that magnesium is both the reason the colour is so green and the reason it is so fragile. Pull the magnesium out and the pigment degrades into a khaki brown within minutes. It is the reason natural greens are rare, the reason copper was added to make the molecule stable, and the reason a clean-label green is still an open formulation problem rather than a solved one.

anthocyanin.title: Anthocyanin — The Colour That Reads the pH
anthocyanin.lede: It is the only natural colour that changes hue on purpose.
anthocyanin.body: Anthocyanins read the acidity of whatever they are dissolved in, and they answer in colour: red in a sports drink, violet in a still water, a dusty pink in a yoghurt. That is not instability — it is a chemical equilibrium doing exactly what it does. It is also why a purple that holds its hue at pH 5 is a technical achievement rather than a matter of luck, and why anthocyanin is usually chosen for the story it tells rather than for the colour it holds still.

betacarotene.title: Beta-Carotene — Orange, Concentrated
betacarotene.lede: One hectare of carrots gives tonnes of pigment. Fermentation gives kilograms.
betacarotene.body: Beta-carotene is the pigment that makes a carrot orange and, for that matter, a mango orange and a pumpkin gold. Extracted from crops it is bound to the harvest; produced by fermentation it is bound to a bioreactor. The molecule is the same in both cases, and so is the colour — which is why the interesting differences show up in assay consistency and supply security rather than in the shade.

stories.cta: Want to go deeper on the science?

science.metaDescription: Natural vs synthetic, sustainability, stability, safety — short, sourced, no jargon.
science.title: Science
science.subtitle: Short, sourced, jargon-free articles on the questions we get asked most.

natural-vs-synthetic.title: Natural vs synthetic dyes
natural-vs-synthetic.lede: They look the same on the page — but they aren't.
natural-vs-synthetic.body: Natural dyes come from plants, minerals, or microbes. Synthetic dyes are made from petrochemicals. The visible difference can be small, but the production footprint, regulatory framework, and skin-sensitisation profile often aren't.

sustainability.title: Are natural pigments sustainable?
sustainability.body: A crop grown for pigment can be a sink for regenerative agriculture, or a monoculture with high water use. Microbial (fermentation) pigments avoid most of the agricultural footprint, but they require energy for fermentation and downstream processing.

stability.title: Stability — why your dye faded
stability.lede: Light, pH, heat, oxygen, and metal ions.
stability.body: Most natural pigments are sensitive to one or more of these. A pigment that's stable in food (pH 4-6, opaque, no light) may fade in a clear cosmetic serum (pH 6-8, light-exposed). This is why formulation matters as much as pigment choice.

safety.title: Are natural pigments safer?
safety.lede: Generally, but "natural" isn't a regulatory category.
safety.body: Some natural pigments (e.g. lawone from henna) are potent skin sensitizers. Some synthetic pigments (e.g. iron oxides) are among the safest colorants we have. The label "natural" tells you origin, not safety.

color-measurement.title: Colour measurement, and what a ΔE actually means
color-measurement.lede: Two batches at the same assay can be different colours.
color-measurement.body: Colour is measured in Lab values and compared with ΔE, and neither number means anything without a method and a substrate attached to it. This is the shortest useful explanation of why the colour on a pigment certificate is not the colour of your product, and of how to close that gap with a written specification rather than with an argument at goods-in.

extraction-vs-fermentation.title: Extraction or fermentation: what actually changes
extraction-vs-fermentation.lede: The same molecule, a different kind of supply risk.
extraction-vs-fermentation.body: A crop-derived pigment and a fermentation-derived pigment are chemically the same compound, and the difference is not in the colour. It is in whether your supply is exposed to a harvest window, a crop yield and a weather season, or whether it is exposed to a controlled bioreactor with a verified assay on every lot. For a buyer, that is the difference between a colour you can plan around and a colour you have to hope for.

clean-label.title: What a clean label actually rules out
clean-label.lede: It is a list of specific exclusions, not a feeling.
clean-label.body: Clean label is neither a legal category nor a single rule. It is a short list of things a label will not carry — synthetic dyes, non-natural chelates, certain carriers, certain processing aids — and the list differs by retailer, by market and by product claim. The useful question is therefore not whether a pigment is natural, but which specific exclusions it collides with.

blue-challenge.title: Why natural blue is so hard
blue-challenge.lede: One commercially available natural food blue, and it comes from a cyanobacterium.
blue-challenge.body: Almost every other hue has several natural sources to choose from. Blue has one: phycocyanin, extracted from spirulina. The reason is chemistry — the chromophore has to absorb strongly in the orange-red part of the spectrum while staying stable enough to survive processing, and very few natural molecules do both at once.
